name: Go
description: Goroutines, channels, interfaces, error handling and the deliberate simplicity that defines the language.

modules.name: Language & Errors
modules.description: Types, interfaces, and Go's explicit approach to failure.

cards.prompt: Why does Go return errors as values instead of throwing?
cards.answer: Because every call site must visibly decide what to do about failure. `if err != nil` is verbose on purpose — error handling is normal control flow, not an exceptional path hidden from the reader.
cards.explanation: Wrap with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` to preserve the chain, then inspect with `errors.Is` (sentinel) or `errors.As` (typed). `panic` is for genuinely unrecoverable programmer errors, not for expected failure.

resources.title: Go blog — Error handling and Go

cards.prompt: How does Go's interface satisfaction differ from Java's?
cards.answer: It is implicit and structural: any type with the right method set satisfies the interface, with no `implements` declaration. Interfaces are therefore usually defined by the *consumer*, not shipped with the implementation.
cards.explanation: That is why 'accept interfaces, return structs' is idiomatic — the caller declares the small interface it needs (often one method) and any existing type can satisfy it. Large interfaces are a smell; `io.Reader` has exactly one method and is everywhere.

cards.prompt: What does this print, and why is it surprising?
cards.explanation: An interface value holds a (type, value) pair. Returning a nil `*MyErr` gives an interface with a non-nil type and a nil value, so it is not equal to nil. Return a literal `nil` for the success path rather than a typed nil pointer.

resources.title: Go FAQ — Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

cards.prompt: Why can `append` here modify the original array?
cards.code:
a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
b := a[:2]           // len 2, cap 5
b = append(b, 99)    // writes into a's backing array
fmt.Println(a)       // [1 2 99 4 5]
cards.answer: A slice is a view — pointer, length, capacity — over a backing array. Because `b` still has spare capacity, `append` writes in place rather than allocating. Use a three-index slice `a[:2:2]` to cap it, or copy explicitly.
cards.explanation: This bites whenever a function receives a slice and appends to it: the caller may or may not see the change, depending on capacity. Slices are cheap to pass precisely because nothing is copied — which is the same reason aliasing is possible.

resources.title: Go blog — Slices: usage and internals

modules.name: Concurrency
modules.description: Goroutines, channels, context and the patterns Go was designed for.

cards.prompt: What is a goroutine, and how does it differ from an OS thread?
cards.answer: A green thread multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime. It starts with a ~2 KB growable stack, so hundreds of thousands are practical, and the runtime scheduler switches them in user space at blocking points.
cards.explanation: That is why Go writes as blocking code but scales like an event loop. The catch is that goroutines are not automatically cleaned up — one blocked forever on a channel is a leak, which is what `context` and buffered/closed channels are for.

cards.answer: An unbuffered channel synchronises sender and receiver — the send blocks until someone receives. A buffered channel accepts up to its capacity without a receiver present.

left.title: make(chan T)
points: Rendezvous: send and receive happen together

right.title: make(chan T, n)
points: Decouples producer and consumer up to n
Hides slow consumers until the buffer fills
Capacity is a real design decision

cards.explanation: 'Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.' That said, a `sync.Mutex` around a struct is often simpler than a channel for guarding shared state — channels are for handing off ownership, not for every lock.

resources.title: Go blog — Share memory by communicating

cards.prompt: What is `context.Context` for, and what is the convention?
cards.answer: Carrying cancellation, deadlines and request-scoped values across API boundaries. Convention: pass it as the first parameter, never store it in a struct, and propagate it into every downstream call.
cards.explanation: When a request is cancelled, the context closes and every goroutine watching `ctx.Done()` can stop — which is how Go avoids leaking work on abandoned requests. A function that accepts a context and ignores it is worse than one that never took it.

cards.answer: It instruments memory accesses and reports data races observed at runtime — two goroutines touching the same memory without synchronisation, where at least one writes.
cards.explanation: It only finds races that actually occur during the run, so it needs tests that exercise concurrency. It is still the single most valuable tool in Go: run the whole suite with `-race` in CI, accepting the slowdown.
